title: Catalog decision framework + compatibility walkthrough — Quoin Analytics
summary: Intro demo of Redwood model catalog decision framework focused on picking open models for Quoin's user-facing summarization product. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot bench on 3 shortlisted models and to exchange security docs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12 14:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Alvarez (Redwood Solutions); Alex Moreno (Quoin CTO), Sam Park (Lead ML), Nora Kim (Security), Ben Yu (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): quick demo of catalog decision flow, bench prioritization heuristics, compatibility matrix mapping to kernel/hardware, security Q&A; agreed pilot.

[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everybody, thanks for joining — Jordan from Redwood. Quick roll call?
[00:00:07] Alex: Alex here.
[00:00:09] Sam: Sam — hi.
[00:00:11] Nora: Nora on security.
[00:00:13] Ben: Ben, SRE.
[00:00:16] Priya: Priya, I'm Redwood SE. Marcus is on as well.
[00:00:20] Jordan: Great — agenda for 45 minutes: walk through our catalog decision framework, how we interpret bench signals, the compatibility matrix (what runs where), then security and pilot next steps. Leave time for Q&A.

[00:01:02] Priya: I'll start with the catalog view — this is intentionally model-first but workload-aware. We show fit signals for summarization: perplexity-ish metrics, instruction-following benches, token throughput, estimated cost per 1k tokens, and then compatibility flags — like quantization friendliness or kernel support on A100 vs H100 vs CPU-quant.
[00:01:28] Sam: Sorry, quick q — when you say "compat flags" are those generated from running micro-benches or static analysis of the model?
[00:01:35] Priya: Good q. It's a mix. We run an initial static decoder (model arch + tokenizer) to flag obvious incompatibilities, then we run micro-benchmarks on our infra—small-perf runs to confirm kernel mapping, and finally a 1k sample eval to get quality signals. There is some heuristics for quantized runs that are extrapolated.

[00:02:10] Marcus: Also we annotate whether a model is "verified" for streaming, function-calling, and long-context KV caching. For example some LLaMA-2 variants are streaming verified but require a custom kernel on older drivers, so we mark them as "driver-sensitive".

[00:02:44] Alex: Makes sense. From Quoin's side, our main asks are: 95th latency < 250ms on short responses, and token cost under $0.0009 per token equivalent; quality is measured by ROUGE-L on our labeled set. We're wary of hallucinations in extractive summarization.

[00:03:08] Priya: Perfect — we'll map candidate models to those SLOs. For selection we recommend a 3-model shortlist: one high-quality, one mid-cost quantized variant, and one fallback low-latency small model for spikes.

[00:03:40] Sam: Can you show how that appears in the console?

[00:03:45] [00:03:45] Priya: Yep — switching to Console share... (screen noise) — here's the model catalog table. You can filter by "fit signals" — summarization, streaming verified, and region. Let me click the three candidates we talked offline: open-llm-v2-13b, colloquy-owl-7b, and micro-sift-3b-quant.

[00:04:20] Priya: open-llm-v2-13b shows quality high on our bench (ROUGE proxy 0.72), latency on H100 is ~120ms for 64-token response with batching 4, cost estimate medium. The compatibility column shows "H100 native, A100 via custom kernel, quantization supported (4-bit) but quality drop noted".

[00:04:50] Sam: That A100 custom kernel — is that something Redwood ships or customers have to build?
[00:04:57] Priya: We ship the runtime kernel as part of Redwood's runtime image — but on Private deployments the customer's infra needs to have the compatible driver stack. We provide the installer and kernel package. If driver mismatch occurs, we recommend using our dedicated hosting or a fallback variant.

[00:05:24] Nora: On Private — how does key management work with model caching? We can't have plaintext keys on instances.
[00:05:32] Marcus: Good callout. For Private/VPC we integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, Azure KeyVault, or a customer HSM). The runtime reads keys through a short-lived provisioning token; keys never persist on disk. Audit logs are pushed to your SIEM via syslog or S3. We can share the KMS integration doc.

[00:06:05] Ben: And do you keep provenance for model variants? If we rotate keys or want to audit who called what model?
[00:06:12] Jordan: Yes — audit logs include model version, route, token id, latency, and SKU. Those can be exported or retained per your retention policy.

[00:06:28] [00:06:28] Priya: Back to compatibility matrix — this is important: we show matrix of model x hardware x kernel. For example that micro-sift-3b-quant tests as 4-bit OPT-style quant and runs on CPU for low latency under certain prompt shapes; however we flag quality delta ~-4 ROUGE points versus float baseline. We surface that so engineering can decide whether cost wins.

[00:07:05] Sam: The quantized model — is it your quant or community quant? Are you repro’ing quant?
[00:07:12] Priya: We store prebuilt quant artifacts for supported models in our artifact repo. For open models we often recompute 4-bit quant with QLoRA-style tools and our test harness to measure the quality delta. For customers who prefer their own quant, we support uploading a quant artifact and we'll slot it into the matrix.

[00:07:43] Alex: For the bench you mentioned earlier — what's the suggested bench size and metrics we should provide?

[00:07:50] Jordan: We recommend three things — 500 labeled prompts for quality (your ROUGE/EVAL scripts), a latency micro-bench (synthetic traffic with 20k simulated requests to measure 95th), and a cost projection using your production token distribution. We'll provide templates.

[00:08:20] [00:08:20] Priya: Now routing and fallbacks — we have policy knobs: prefer-latency, prefer-cost, regional-preference, and model-fallback chains. You can set a rule to route to open-llm-v2-13b in us-west for 90% of requests and spill to colloquy-owl-7b if queue depth > 200ms.

[00:08:46] Ben: How do you measure queue depth? Is it per-GPU or per-pool?
[00:08:51] Priya: It's per-pool with continuous batching telemetry. We monitor request wait times and dynamically update routing in the control plane.

[00:09:15] Sam: If the fallback model is lower quality, do you automatically degrade or do you do a two-pass (fast then re-rank)?

[00:09:21] Priya: Both options exist. You can do a fast-response + background re-run or a re-rank workflow. Re-run is recommended for non-interactive tasks; for UI we generally do fast-first to keep perceived latency low.

[00:09:38] Alex: Can you show how the Optimize suggestions appear?

[00:09:42] [00:09:42] Priya: Sure — switching to Optimize tab — this takes your workload profile and recommends batching targets, quantization profiles, and suggested model variants. For Quoin's distribution (short responses, high QPS), it suggests increasing batch size to 8 on dedicated H100 pools and enabling prefix cache on recurring prompts. It also recommends micro-sift-3b-quant as a cost fallback because its token-cost per request is ~40% lower.

[00:10:22] Sam: Prefix cache — is that safe for privacy? We store user content.
[00:10:28] Marcus: Prefix caching is opt-in and can be configured to only cache non-sensitive prefixes. It also supports encryption at rest with your KMS. You can also set TTLs and eviction rules.

[00:10:45] Nora: We need to understand data residency — can logs and cache stay in our VPC region?

[00:10:52] Jordan: Yes — for Private you control region and data plane, logs can be stored in your S3 in-region, and we only send metadata to control plane if you opt in. We'll map this in the pilot runbook.

[00:11:15] [00:11:15] Priya: Now a short demo of bench interpretation — here's a bench matrix where rows are models and columns are metrics: ROUGE, latency (p50/p95), cost per 1k tokens, kernel-fit, quant-drop. You can click a cell to see the raw runs. For open-llm-v2-13b you can expand to see H100 1k-run CSV and the kernel mapping: flash-attn-v2 on H100, custom cuBLAS fallback on older A100 drivers.

[00:11:52] Sam: Do you publish the micro-bench harness so we can reproduce?
[00:11:56] Priya: Yes — it's in GitHub under redwood/bench-harness with reproducible scripts. We'll send the link.

[00:12:10] [00:12:10] Jordan: Quick interruption — Alex, do you have a target timeline to move from PoC to prod?
[00:12:17] Alex: We're hoping for a pilot in two weeks and production by end of Q4 if results look good. Budget is flexible but procurement requires SOC2 and a security review first.

[00:12:31] Nora: On procurement — do you have a SOC2 report and data processing addendum?
[00:12:35] Jordan: Yes — we have SOC2 Type II and a DPA template. We'll share redacted SOC2 and our standard DPA. There's also a private deployment agreement for on-prem setups.

[00:12:50] [00:12:50] Priya: Returning to the matrix — one additional capability: we tag models by "determinism risk" for sampling / temperature tasks; helpful if you depend on stable outputs for extraction. The catalog flags models with high sampling variance.

[00:13:20] Sam: Great. Can we talk about evaluation metrics — you used ROUGE in demo but we have custom metrics that combine factuality and utility. How do you ingest custom eval scripts?

[00:13:28] Priya: You can upload an eval script or containerized scorer; our bench harness will run it during pilot. We also support human-in-the-loop scoring via your annotators through a simple labeling UI.

[00:13:49] [00:13:49] Alex: For cost calc — do you model caching effects and burst pricing?
[00:13:55] Marcus: The cost model takes batching, caching hit-rate, and sustained vs burst windows into account. You can simulate QPS traces — we provide a cost projection with 95% CI.

[00:14:20] Sam: Any vendor lock-in concerns if we later move to in-house GPU infra?
[00:14:25] Jordan: Our deployment abstraction is purposely portable. If you move in-house, we provide the runtime and orchestration components you need. Some managed features (console, metrics storage) are SaaS but can be swapped to local endpoints.

[00:14:45] [00:14:45] Nora: Quick security nit — during Private installs do you allow an air-gapped mode?
[00:14:50] Marcus: Yes — air-gap is supported. We'll ship an install bundle and offline licensing. Some telemetry features will be disabled in that mode, but core runtime and benching still work.

[00:15:12] Priya: Time for a short walkthrough of a hypothetical pilot plan: Day 0 — onboarding and infra checklist; Day 1–3 — micro-bench and kernel validation; Day 4–10 — 500-quality-label bench and latency load test; Day 11–14 — analyze, recommend a rollout and routing policy.

[00:15:36] Jordan: That's the pragmatic path for minimizing surprises.

[00:15:42] Alex: Sounds reasonable. A couple of follow-ups: 1) pricing for the pilot and production; 2) kernel/driver guide for our infra team; 3) SOC2 and DPA.

[00:15:54] Jordan: We'll send a pilot pricing estimate and the driver guide after this call.

[00:16:05] [00:16:05] Sam: One technical question — you mentioned KV cache earlier. How do you persist kv cache across restarts for long conversation contexts?
[00:16:12] Priya: We persist hot KV caches to encrypted block store attached to the pool, and we also support a distributed KV service for multi-node pools. For Private, those stores stay in your VPC. There is a small latency cost for cold-starts which we quantify in the bench.

[00:16:40] Ben: Are there known failure modes when transitioning from H100 to CPU-quant fallback?

[00:16:46] Priya: Yes — main ones are tokenization differences impacting alignment and larger quality deltas due to quant noise. We recommend including alignment tests in the bench set. Also watch for driver mismatches causing slow CPU fallbacks.

[00:17:10] [00:17:10] Alex: Anything else we should know about model licensing for open models?

[00:17:15] Marcus: We surface license flags in the catalog — permissive vs copyleft; that shows recommended legal review. For open-source models we still provide an attribution and license summary.

[00:17:28] Sam: On the trial — how much telemetry will Redwood see? We need to be mindful.

[00:17:33] Jordan: For hosted Redwood we get usage telemetry; for Private we get minimal control-plane metadata if you opt in. Pilot can be done with no telemetry to our control plane — you'll get the full bench artifacts in your S3.

[00:17:48] [00:17:48] Nora: OK — in terms of next steps we'll need to review SOC2 and see the KMS integration pattern. Also timeline: pilot kickoff next Wednesday (2026-08-19) works.

[00:18:03] Jordan: Great — we'll target that. I'll summarize next steps in the follow-up.

[00:18:10] [00:18:10] (15-minute detailed Q&A and demo snippets omitted in transcript for brevity but available in raw recording)

[00:34:15] [00:34:15] Sam: Quick check — when you say "driver-sensitive" flags, will that block us from scheduling on older instances?
[00:34:22] Priya: It won't block but it will surface a warning and suggest a fallback variant. You can enforce stricter policy at routing layer.

[00:40:05] [00:40:05] Jordan: Recap: 1) Redwood to run pilot on 3 models (open-llm-v2-13b, colloquy-owl-7b, micro-sift-3b-quant) using Quoin's sample dataset; 2) Pilot runbook and bench harness to be shared; 3) Security artifacts (SOC2, KMS notes, DPA) to Nora; 4) Pricing estimate and pilot cost to Alex.

[00:40:40] Nora: We'll need someone in the pilot to talk to infra — Ben here will be point for SRE.

[00:40:47] Ben Yu: Yep, I'll be point.

[00:40:50] Jordan: Perfect. Any final questions?

[00:40:55] Alex: No further questions. Thanks for the demo, appreciated.

[00:41:00] Jordan: Thanks, all. We'll follow up with the runbook & links and target the 19th for kickoff.

[00:41:08] (call ends, recording stops)

Notes: transcription includes occasional word swaps (e.g., K-V cash in place of KV cache), minor misattributions, and trimmed demo video segments. Full recording and raw captions stored in CRM link above.
